However, for sake of argument, if for some reason they couldn't pay the full cost, I'd argue that they (the parents/family) shouldn't be detained. My reasoning is as follows: in the business world, you take a risk every time you sell a product. It usually takes around 30 days for payment to arrive, that's normal, and there is a risk that the company will go broke during that time, or they simply won't pay if they think they can get away with it. In this case you'd take them to court, or negotiate a percentage of debt owed, you may even sell that debt to a debt collector for a certain percentage of the total amount. You don't send them to Jail if their only crime is not being able to pay; you don't hold their employees hostage; you don't get them to enter into a contract to pay you back everything they make for the rest of their life until the debt is paid.

In this case, you want your kid to live, the hospital also wants him to live, and doesn't want the very bad press of letting a baby die. But, they also want money. If the price is too high, and the parents genuinely can't afford to pay: the kid dies, the parents are upset and create a shit-storm, the hospital gets in a lot of shit. If the price is too high, and the parents can't afford to pay, but they continue to provide care for the child, it's costing them money, that isn't going to be repaid, more money in the long run than if they palmed the baby off to a US hospital. If the price is too low, the hospital misses out on profit, or makes a loss. It's in no-one's interest to keep the kid there, everyone loses. So you find a middle ground.

The hospital is well within their right to demand any price. But they deserve all the bad press they're getting. And if it gets bad enough that it makes a sizeable dint in Mexico's tourism industry, then they deserve all the flak they get from the cartel government.
